title: Arabian Coffee Culture
summary: How Arabic coffee, or qahwa, is prepared with cardamom and saffron, served with dates, and used as a sign of hospitality and respect toward guests.
poll: The way a family serves coffee to guests says as much about their culture as the coffee itself.

versions.title: Arabian Coffee Culture
versions.text:
In many homes, hot coffee is a sign of a warm welcome. Folks call this drink qahwa. It is served to guests with care.

First, beans are roasted. The beans turn light brown. Next, the beans are ground. This makes a fine powder. The powder is boiled in water. This is done in a tall pot.

Most homes add a spice to the pot. This spice is cardamom. It has a strong smell. Some homes add a bit more spice, too. This one is called saffron. It gives the drink a gold hue.

The coffee is poured into tiny cups. A host pours for each guest. The host fills the cup just part way. The cup is not filled all the way up.

Dates are set out, too. A date is sweet. A date can calm the bold taste. Guests take a date with their cup.

This way to serve coffee is an old custom. It shows guests they are welcome. A host who serves it well is seen as kind.

Many homes still serve qahwa this way today. It links each guest to an old way of life.

versions.title: Arabian Coffee Culture
versions.text:
In many homes across Arabia, coffee is an immediate sign of a warm welcome. This special coffee is called qahwa. It is served to guests with great care, a true mark of local hospitality.

Preparing qahwa begins with roasting coffee beans slowly over low heat until they turn a light, golden brown. The roasting fills the house with a rich aroma. Once roasted, the beans are ground into a fine powder. This powder is then boiled with water. It is boiled in a tall, curved pot called a dallah, used for this purpose across the region for centuries.

Most families add a few crushed cardamom pods to the pot while it boils. Cardamom is a spice with a strong, pleasant smell that fills a room. Some families also stir in a tiny pinch of saffron. This gives the coffee a golden color and a sweet scent.

The finished coffee is poured into small, handleless cups called finjan. A host moves carefully around the room, pouring a cup for each guest. The host often starts with the eldest or most honored guest. The host usually fills each cup only part way, a sign of thoughtful care.

Dates are almost always set out beside the coffee. A sweet, soft date balances the coffee's strong taste. Many guests take a date before or after each sip.

This ritual of serving coffee is a longstanding tradition. It is carried faithfully from one generation to the next. It shows guests that they are genuinely welcome. A host who performs it well is seen as generous and polite.

Today, families across Arabia keep this same careful ritual for every guest. It connects each new guest to a tradition many years old.

MID.modelAnswer: I think starting with the eldest or most honored guest shows the most hospitality. Filling the cup only part way and offering dates both matter too, but they are shown to every guest equally, while serving order singles out respect for a particular person.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how two specific elements of the qahwa ritual, such as a particular gesture, spice, or serving order, work together to express the region's heritage of hospitality. Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained two specific elements of the ritual accurately.
I connected each element to the region's heritage of hospitality.

HIGH.modelAnswer: Two elements that express this heritage of hospitality are the serving order and the gesture used to decline a refill. The article explains that a host moves around the room serving the eldest or most honored guest first, a gesture rooted in longstanding cultural practice around respect and seniority; this quiet choice communicates who the host is honoring without anyone needing to say a word. Likewise, a guest can gently shake an empty cup to decline more coffee, a subtle gesture that lets the ritual continue smoothly without an awkward spoken refusal. Because this entire ritual existed long before any written etiquette guide, both elements show how oral tradition and shared, unspoken understanding were enough to carry a culture's values of respect and generosity across many generations.
